title: Lori Trahan — Campaign loans and disclosures
outcome: Committee dismissed. No excessive contribution found and no further action on corrected disclosures.
summary: The House Ethics Committee concluded the campaign loans came from Trahan’s personal funds. It found no evidence that the disclosure errors or omissions were knowing and willful, noted that she amended the disclosures, and voted to dismiss on July 15, 2020. The matter closed with publication on July 16. Separately, in MURs 7585 and 7588, the FEC found no reason to believe Trahan knowingly accepted excessive contributions and exercised prosecutorial discretion to dismiss certain reporting and deposit allegations involving her campaign committee and treasurer.

title: Rashida Tlaib — 2018 campaign salary
outcome: Committee directed $10,800 in repayment. FEC documented repayment and dismissed the allegations.
summary: The House Ethics Committee found that $10,800 covered periods after Tlaib ceased to be a candidate and directed her to reimburse her campaign. It found she did not seek to enrich herself unjustly. The Committee voted on July 23, 2020 to take no further action, with closure subject to confirmation of compliance. The FEC later documented reimbursement and dismissed the allegations in MUR 7579 under its prosecutorial discretion.

additional_sources.label: FEC approved factual and legal analysis

title: Roger Williams — FAST Act amendment
outcome: No House rule or law violated. Committee dismissed.
summary: OCE referred the matter on May 13, 2016. The Committee reviewed whether Williams sponsored an amendment that affected auto dealerships, including his own. It found that sponsorship did not violate a law or House rule, advised that he should have sought guidance, and unanimously dismissed the matter.

title: David Schweikert — House reprimand and fine
outcome: House reprimand and $50,000 fine. Separate FEC settlements involved the campaign committee and a former staffer.
summary: The House Ethics Committee investigated referrals received in 2018. Schweikert admitted 11 violations involving campaign finance and disclosure, official resources and staff, and lack of candor. On July 31, 2020, the House adopted the Committee report under H.Res. 1074, reprimanding Schweikert and imposing a $50,000 fine. In FEC MUR 7923, the campaign committee and former staffer Richard Oliver Schwab separately agreed to civil penalties of $125,000 and $7,500, respectively.

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — 2021 Met Gala gifts and payments
outcome: Gift-rule and oversight findings. Additional payments directed, with closure subject to confirmation.
summary: The Committee found that Ocasio-Cortez accepted impermissible gifts related to her attire and her guest’s free admission to the 2021 Met Gala, that vendor payments were delayed, and that she failed to exercise proper oversight over staff. It noted her proactive compliance efforts and found no evidence that she intentionally underpaid. It did not find that the violations were knowing and willful and did not deem a sanction necessary. It directed an additional $2,733.28 payment to Brother Vellies and a $250 donation to the Costume Institute for her guest’s meal, with closure subject to confirmation of payment.

title: Jimmy Gomez — House conduct report
outcome: Committee found violations of clauses 1 and 18(b). Any House sanction requires separate House action.
summary: The Committee announced its review on August 17, 2026. In a report adopted November 19 and released November 23, 2026, the House Ethics Committee found that Gomez violated clauses 1 and 18(b) of the Code of Official Conduct by making unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer. Gomez maintained that the contact was consensual. The Committee left any sanction to the House.

title: Mike Kelly — Cleveland-Cliffs stock purchase review
category: Confidential information and conflict of interest
outcome: Committee reproval. Divestment and donation of any divestment profits recommended.
summary: The Committee did not find evidence that Kelly knowingly or intentionally caused his spouse to trade on inside information, found no clear conflict-of-interest violation, and could not determine whether her purchase was improper. It found that Kelly violated clause 1 of the Code of Official Conduct, including by failing to meet his duty of candor. The report adopted July 22, 2025 served as a reproval. It recommended divestment before further official action directly related to Cleveland-Cliffs and donation to charity of any divestment profits.

title: Wesley Hunt — Campaign spending review
outcome: Committee closed the inquiry and took no further action.
summary: The Committee received an OCE referral on March 25, 2024 and published it with Hunt’s response on June 24. On December 30, 2024, the Committee announced it had unanimously closed several matters, including Hunt’s. It said it found no evidence that any member intentionally misused campaign funds for personal benefit. The statement did not attribute its group-level compliance concerns to Hunt individually.

title: Ronny Jackson — Campaign spending review
outcome: Committee closed the inquiry and took no further action.
summary: The Committee received OCE referrals on December 22, 2021 and March 25, 2024 about the same campaign spending allegations and released referral materials in May 2022 and June 2024. On December 30, 2024, it announced it had unanimously closed several matters, including Jackson’s. It said it found no evidence that any member intentionally misused campaign funds for personal benefit. The statement did not attribute its group-level compliance concerns to Jackson individually.

title: Gwen Moore — 2014 protest citation review
outcome: Committee declined to impanel an investigative subcommittee.
summary: Moore received a disorderly conduct citation following a September 4, 2014 protest in West Milwaukee. The Committee considered the matter on September 10 and declined to form an investigative subcommittee. Its report described a prospective fine. Final court disposition and payment were not confirmed.

title: Pat Fallon — Periodic transaction report review
outcome: Committee unanimously dismissed the referral after remedial steps.
summary: OCE referred Fallon’s periodic transaction reports on March 2, 2022. The Committee extended review on April 18 and released referral materials on May 31. The Committee found no clear evidence the errors and omissions were knowing or willful, noted remedial efforts, and dismissed the referral.

title: Victoria Spartz — Airport citation review
outcome: Virginia charge dismissed and TSA civil penalty paid, as reported by the Committee. Committee closed its review.
summary: The Committee reported that Spartz was cited at Dulles on June 28, 2024 for traveling through security with an unloaded handgun and was charged on July 11. Spartz told the Committee she completed a gun-safety course. The report states she paid a separate TSA civil penalty and that the Virginia charge was dismissed by nolle prosequi on September 20. The Committee declined to form a subcommittee and closed its review.

title: Al Green — 2021 protest arrest review
outcome: Committee took no further action.
summary: The Committee considered Green’s August 3, 2021 protest-related arrest and declined to form a subcommittee. The Committee reported that Green intended to pay $50 and that local proceedings were expected to end without further action. The Committee closed its own matter on publication.

title: Gregory W. Meeks — Loan and disclosure review
outcome: Committee closed its investigation. Disclosure noncompliance was inadvertent. The improper-gift allegation was not substantiated.
summary: After a May 2011 OCE referral, the Committee dismissed allegations concerning the separate investment-firm loan. It found that Meeks had inadvertently omitted the $40,000 Ahmad loan from two financial disclosures, which he later amended. It closed the improper-gift inquiry after it could not substantiate that allegation.

title: Ilhan Omar — Financial disclosure and book advance review
outcome: OCE recommended dismissal and transmitted no findings. Committee ended review.
summary: The Committee received the OCE referral on December 22, 2021 about financial disclosure and a possible book advance. OCE unanimously recommended dismissal and transmitted no findings. A majority of the Committee did not vote to dismiss, but the Committee stated that it would not review the matter further.

title: Pramila Jayapal — 2018 protest arrest review
outcome: Committee took no further action. Local charge disposed of after $50 collateral forfeiture.
summary: The Committee considered Jayapal’s June 28, 2018 protest-related arrest. It reported that she forfeited $50 in collateral and that the local court disposed of the charge. The Committee declined to form an investigative subcommittee and closed the matter.

title: Chuck Edwards — House censure
outcome: House censured Edwards on September 1, 2026.
summary: The Committee publicly announced its review on May 14, 2026. The House Ethics Committee adopted its report on July 22, 2026 and recommended censure. It found that Edwards violated clauses 1 and 2 of the Code of Official Conduct through conduct contrary to the spirit of the House’s prohibition on sexual harassment and unwanted advances. Edwards cooperated with the investigation, disputed the findings and waived procedural steps required for the Committee to recommend a floor sanction. The House adopted H.Res. 1498 on September 1, 413–2, and censured him.

additional_sources.label: House Ethics censure recommendation and findings

title: Troy E. Nehls — Campaign finance reproval
outcome: Committee adopted a report serving as a reproval.
summary: The Committee received an OCE referral on December 11, 2023 and reviewed campaign rent and payments through Nehls’s company, Liberty 1776. It found the unregistered entity’s role led to improper contributions, incomplete reporting and expenditures whose campaign purpose could not be verified. Nehls disputed some factual and legal conclusions and noted the report’s treatment of recordkeeping discrepancies as inadvertent. The Committee adopted the report as a reproval on November 19, 2026 and closed the matter on publication.

title: Judy Chu — Public letter of reproval
outcome: Committee issued a public letter of reproval.
summary: The Committee found that two senior staffers directed limited campaign work using official resources. It found no evidence Chu knew of that improper use. It found that Chu’s communications with staff interfered with the inquiry and violated House rules. It noted her expression of regret, issued a public letter of reproval and closed the matter on publication.

title: Joyce Beatty — 2021 protest arrest review
outcome: Committee took no further action. Beatty reported paying $50.
summary: The Committee considered Beatty’s July 15, 2021 protest-related arrest and declined to form a subcommittee. Beatty told the Committee she had paid $50 before release. The Committee closed its review upon publication.

title: Sam Graves — Committee hearing witness review
outcome: Committee found no House rule or standard of conduct violated.
summary: After an August 2009 OCE referral, the Committee reviewed Graves’ approval of a hearing witness who had investments in common with his wife. The Committee found no applicable rule or standard was violated and identified no evidence that the hearing or testimony resulted in action that could benefit Graves, his wife, or the witness.

title: Judy Chu — 2022 protest arrest review
outcome: Committee took no further action.
summary: The Committee considered Chu’s June 30, 2022 protest-related arrest and declined to form a subcommittee. It reported that Chu intended to pay $50 and that local proceedings were expected to end without further action. The Committee closed its own matter upon publication.

title: Maxine Waters — OneUnited Bank review
outcome: Committee found no violation by Waters. Her chief of staff received a separate reproval.
summary: After an OCE referral, the Committee and outside counsel reviewed Waters’s request for a Treasury meeting. The Committee concluded that Waters did not violate any applicable House rule, law, regulation or standard of conduct. It issued a separate letter of reproval to her chief of staff, Mikael Moore, for his actions regarding OneUnited.

title: Bill Huizenga — Campaign recordkeeping
outcome: Committee found a recordkeeping-related House rule violation and closed the matter without a sanction.
summary: The House Ethics Committee found that inadequate campaign recordkeeping violated clause 6 of the Code of Official Conduct. It did not find clear personal use of campaign funds by Huizenga. The Committee noted his cooperation and corrective steps, sent a private letter with its findings and expectations, and took no further action without imposing a sanction.

title: Mike Collins — Intern compensation and staff oversight
outcome: Committee closed the matter after agreeing with Collins on a $2,880 return to Treasury for intern compensation.
summary: The Committee found that Collins’s congressional office improperly paid an intern and accepted improper voluntary services. It identified potentially improper travel reimbursements involving a staffer but did not find substantial evidence that his office misused its Members’ Representational Allowance for that travel. Collins and the Committee agreed that $2,880 would be returned to the Treasury for the intern compensation, and the Committee closed the matter.

title: Lauren Boebert — House chamber mask rule fine (February 15, 2022)
outcome: Fine notice published after appeal period expired.
summary: The Committee received notice on February 15, 2022 that the Sergeant at Arms fined Boebert under H. Res. 38, the House chamber mask rule. The Committee reported that Boebert did not appeal by the deadline.

outcome: Appeal did not receive majority support.

title: Thomas R. Suozzi — Periodic transaction report review
outcome: Committee unanimously dismissed the referral after remedial steps.
summary: The Committee received an OCE referral on February 28, 2022 concerning timely periodic transaction reports. It extended review in April and released the referral and Suozzi’s response on July 29. The Committee unanimously dismissed the referral after finding no clear evidence the errors or omissions were knowing or willful and noting remedial efforts.
